what: Object storage keeps files (photos, videos, backups, logs) as whole objects in buckets, each found by a key. It is cheap, almost endless, and very hard to lose data from.
like: Like a huge coat check: you hand over a bag, get a ticket (the key), and later swap the ticket for the exact same bag.
why: Stores any amount of data at low cost, with no disks for you to manage
Built to keep data safe: 11 nines of durability across separate data centres
Browsers upload directly with presigned URLs, and analytics engines read it as a data lake

steps.d: Your API checks who the user is, then signs a presigned URL: a link that allows one action on one key for a short time. No cloud keys reach the browser.
The browser PUTs the file to the bucket over HTTPS. Big files (from about 100 MB) go as a multipart upload: parts in parallel, retried one by one, then joined.
An object is the bytes plus metadata (name-value pairs like content type), found by bucket and key. You never edit part of it - you replace the whole object.
S3 Standard keeps copies across several Availability Zones (separate data centres). Once a write succeeds, every read and list sees it straight away - strong read-after-write consistency.
A new object can send an event to a queue, topic or Lambda - for example to make thumbnails. Delivery is at least once, so handlers should be safe to repeat.
Versioning keeps old copies so a bad overwrite or delete can be undone. Lifecycle rules move old objects to cheaper, colder classes, then delete them on a schedule.

numbers.l: writes / reads per second per prefix, at least
max parts in one multipart upload, each 5 MiB to 5 GiB
longest life of a presigned URL made with the CLI

choices.d: Request limits apply per prefix (the start of the key). Spread hot traffic over many prefixes, e.g. users/42/... or a short hash first, and you can scale reads and writes in parallel.
Standard for hot files. Colder classes cost less to store but more to read and have a minimum stay - on GCS 30 days for Nearline, 90 for Coldline, 365 for Archive.
Move objects to colder classes as they age, delete temp uploads after a few days, and expire old versions so versioning does not grow your bill forever.
Small files: one PUT. Big files: multipart with parallel parts and retries. From the browser: presigned URLs, so your servers never carry the bytes.
Used as a data lake, store analytics data as columnar files (like Parquet) under prefixes such as date=2026-10-28/, so query engines like Spark or Athena read only the slices they need.

instead.why: Sits in front of the bucket to serve popular files fast worldwide
For small structured rows you query, filter and update in place
Millisecond lookups of small items that change often
Fast SQL analytics over data you load from the lake

breaks.d: Every upload lands under one prefix, like today's date, so requests pile up on one slice.
breaks.see: 503 Slow Down errors and rising latency on PUTs
breaks.fix: Spread keys over many prefixes and retry with backoff

breaks.d: A single PUT of a huge file restarts from zero on any network blip.
breaks.see: Long uploads failing near the end, users retrying
breaks.fix: Multipart upload with parallel parts that retry on their own

breaks.d: Multipart uploads that never complete leave stored parts behind.
breaks.see: Storage bill higher than the objects you can list
breaks.fix: A lifecycle rule that aborts incomplete multipart uploads after a few days

breaks.d: Events are delivered at least once and can arrive late or out of order.
breaks.fix: Make handlers idempotent (safe to repeat), keyed by object key and version

breaks.d: A Lambda triggered by uploads writes its output back to the same bucket and triggers itself.
breaks.see: Invocations and objects climbing without end
breaks.fix: Write output to another bucket or prefix, and filter the trigger by prefix

say: Media goes in object storage, not the database - the database keeps only the key, size and owner for each file.
Clients upload straight to the bucket with a presigned URL from my API, so large files never pass through my servers, and big ones use multipart upload.
An ObjectCreated event goes to a queue, and workers make thumbnails or transcode video, with idempotent handlers because delivery is at least once.
A CDN serves reads, versioning protects against bad deletes, and lifecycle rules move old files to colder, cheaper classes.

followups.q: How do you let users upload a 5 GB video?
followups.a: The API creates a multipart upload and returns presigned URLs for each part. The client sends parts in parallel, retries failed ones, then calls complete. A lifecycle rule cleans up uploads that never finish.

followups.q: Can you read a file right after writing it?
followups.a: Yes. S3 has strong read-after-write consistency for new writes, overwrites, deletes and lists, at no extra cost. A CDN in front can still serve an old copy until its cache time runs out.

followups.q: How would you handle 50,000 reads per second?
followups.a: Each prefix supports at least 5,500 reads per second, so spread keys over 10 or more prefixes and read in parallel. Put a CDN in front so most reads never reach the bucket.

followups.q: Why not store images in the database?
followups.a: Big blobs bloat backups and replicas and waste expensive database memory and I/O. Object storage is cheaper per GB, scales on its own and plugs into CDNs. Keep the key in the database.

today: Since December 2025 a single S3 object can be up to 50 TB, ten times the old 5 TB limit, which helps with large video and AI training files.

check.q: How should a browser upload a large file without passing through your servers?
check.a: With a presigned URL from your API
d: By sending your cloud access keys to the browser
By emailing it to a worker
check.why: A presigned URL allows one action on one key for a short time, so the browser can upload safely on its own.

check.q: All uploads go under one prefix and you start seeing 503 Slow Down. What helps most?
d: Move to a colder storage class
check.why: Request limits apply per prefix, so more prefixes means more parallel capacity.

check.q: You need to change one line inside a 2 GB object. What really happens?
check.a: You upload a whole new object to replace it
d: S3 patches just that byte range
S3 locks the object and edits it on disk
check.why: Objects are written as a whole. With versioning on, the old copy stays as an earlier version.

check.q: Your thumbnail worker made two thumbnails for one upload. Why?
check.a: Events are delivered at least once
d: Multipart uploads always send two events
check.why: Duplicates can happen, so handlers should be idempotent.
